summary:
Caribbean Netherlands comprises Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law on civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination extends to the islands, and the statutory framework operating in the European Netherlands applies here in the same form.

That protection covers visitors as well as residents. Travel-facing coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023 ranks Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, on the stated basis that as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are covered by strict anti-discrimination laws and that same-sex couples are warmly welcomed.

Same-sex unions have been registrable since 2012. On 4 December 2012 the Census Office in Saba recorded the Caribbean Netherlands' first: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, wed Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on the island; both were visiting, which establishes a local record of performing same-sex unions for people who are only passing through.

Ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry. The official weddings page of Saba Tourism identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony and documents registrar Julieta Woods as flexible with couples' wishes, alongside a full destination-wedding supply chain of caterers, florists and accommodation.

No source in the current inventory addresses gender-marker rules on identity documents, entry screening practice, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and harassment exposure for trans visitors specifically; the findings above rest on marriage and anti-discrimination provisions rather than trans-specific legal text.
tangentialFactors:
The strongest positive indicator in the inventory is a ranking rather than a legal instrument: GayCities places Bonaire fifth in a regional top ten, an assessment made by a travel publication on the strength of Dutch anti-discrimination law and marriage equality, not a finding of a court or ministry.

The equality-friendly reputation documented for Bonaire rests on provisions that protect on the basis of sexual orientation and status generally. Nothing in the inventory shows how those provisions are applied when a trans person is the complainant, or whether enforcement bodies treat gender identity as a protected ground in practice on the islands.

The 2012 Saba registration and the Saba Tourism wedding material both concern same-sex couples. They evidence an administrative willingness to process unions for people who are not resident, which is a useful indicator of registry openness, but they say nothing about how registry staff handle a applicant whose presentation differs from the sex recorded on their documents.
localsOnly:
Residents of the three special municipalities are covered by Dutch national anti-discrimination law, and the same statutory framework as the European Netherlands applies without local modification.

The Saba registry performs civil ceremonies as routine business. Saba Tourism documents the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony, names registrar Julieta Woods as flexible with couples' wishes, and lists local caterers, florists and accommodation able to service a wedding.

The Census Office in Saba has processed a same-sex union since 4 December 2012, giving the island a documented administrative history of registering such unions.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in the inventory addresses gender-marker change or amendment rules on Dutch identity documents as applied in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius or Saba, including whether a visitor can obtain a document matching their lived gender while in the territory.

Unresolved: entry and border screening practice is not sourced. Whether immigration officers at the islands' ports of entry ask about gender identity, or flag passport/ presentation mismatches, is not documented here.

Unresolved: access to gender-affirming care on the three islands, including hormone therapy continuity and referral pathways to the European Netherlands, is not covered by any source in the inventory.

Unresolved: facilities access (restrooms, accommodation, beaches) and harassment exposure for trans visitors specifically are not sourced. The anti-discrimination protection cited is general statutory text; its enforcement record in trans-specific cases on the islands is not documented.

Unresolved: no trans-specific legal text, court decision or official guidance from Bonaire, Sint Eustatius or Saba appears in the inventory. The positive findings derive from marriage and anti-discrimination provisions extended from Dutch national law.
